title-group.article-title: Pathologic and radiologic response to neoadjuvant therapy in advanced differentiated thyroid cancer

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Neoadjuvant therapies for locally advanced differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) aim to downstage disease and thereby reduce the extent of surgical resection without compromising oncologic results. Understanding the histopathologic changes induced by these therapies and their correlation with radiologic response may refine surgical planning and guide optimal treatment protocols.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To characterize the histopathologic effects of neoadjuvant therapies on locally advanced DTC and evaluate their association with radiologic response and surgical outcomes.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This is a retrospective case series of patients with initially unresectable, locally advanced DTC treated with neoadjuvant therapies, lenvatinib or dabrafenib/trametinib. All patients underwent comprehensive clinical, radiologic, and histopathologic evaluation before and after neoadjuvant therapy. Histopathologic response was assessed on resection specimens using hematoxylin–eosin staining and immunohistochemistry staining for CD3, CD31, and ERG. The primary outcomes were histopathologic response, including tumor fibrosis, tumor necrosis, vascular density, and immune cell infiltration. Secondary outcomes included radiologic response, surgical feasibility, and perioperative morbidity.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: All nine patients achieved sufficient tumor regression to allow surgical resection. Histopathology demonstrated therapy-induced tumor fibrosis and necrosis as the predominant changes. Lenvatinib-treated tumors exhibited marked vascular remodeling, reduced microvessel density, and prominent lymphocytic infiltration, whereas BRAF-targeted therapy primarily induced tumor fibrosis without similar vascular or immune changes. The neoadjuvant therapy was well tolerated and did not increase surgical morbidity.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Neoadjuvant therapy facilitated R0 resection of locally advanced DTC. Lenvatinib induced vascular remodeling and immune infiltration, in contrast to fibrosis primarily seen with dabrafenib/trametinib. These histologic differences may have implications for future therapeutic decision-making.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Thyroid cancer is typically associated with favorable outcomes. Surgical resection with the addition of radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation or external beam radiation therapy when indicated usually results in high cure rates (1). However, in cases of advanced thyroid cancer, tumor invasion into adjacent vital structures can be surgically challenging and associated with potentially considerable morbidity. Recent advancements in systemic therapies have shifted treatment paradigms for advanced thyroid cancer patients, particularly for patients with radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC). The introduction of multitarget tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), including sorafenib and lenvatinib, has significantly improved progression-free survival in this patient population (2, 3).

Encouraged by the efficacy of adjuvant systemic therapies, there has been growing interest in their application in the neoadjuvant context for patients with locally advanced unresectable thyroid cancer. Several studies have reported promising results. For instance, a phase II trial investigating anlotinib – a multitarget TKI – demonstrated a substantial tumor response, enabling R0/R1 resections in 8 out of 13 patients (4). In addition, a recent multicenter Latin American case series by Pitoia et al. (5) reported outcomes of neoadjuvant therapy in 27 patients with locally advanced thyroid cancer treated with multikinase inhibitors or selective targeted agents. In that cohort, neoadjuvant therapy enabled surgical intervention in 55% of patients with DTC, with R0/R1 resection achieved in 60% of those undergoing surgery.

Neoadjuvant treatment offers a unique opportunity to evaluate histopathologic changes that reflect therapeutic response in surgical specimens. A prior study has demonstrated that pathologic assessment after neoadjuvant therapy can yield important insights into treatment response and tumor biology (6). Further exploring this concept, a detailed evaluation of the pathologic response may further elucidate drug mechanisms, tumor biology, and potential biomarkers of efficacy. In this study, we aimed to characterize the histopathologic changes of the tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment induced by neoadjuvant therapy, focusing upon vascular remodeling, angiogenesis, immune infiltration, and residual tumor cell viability.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The Ethics Committee of Institutional Review Board of Tel-Aviv Sourasky Medical Center approved the retrospective analysis of anonymized patient data (approval number: IRB TLV-0902-20). Patient consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study, and all data were anonymized prior to analysis.

All of the included patients were treated at the Head and Neck Oncology Unit of the Tel-Aviv Sourasky Medical Center between January 2023 and January 2025. Included were patients with advanced DTC initially deemed unresectable or those in whom surgical resection would have resulted in a considerable risk of morbidity. Disease staging was determined in accordance with the AJCC 8th edition. Neoadjuvant treatment initiation was decided upon by a multidisciplinary team discussion.

The therapeutic regimen selection was tailored to each patient according to molecular and genetic changes detected via core-needle biopsy specimens. Tumor samples were analyzed using the Oncomine Comprehensive Assay (OCA), a targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) assay to simultaneously detect and identify mutations and fusions of over 500 genes associated with cancer, as previously reported (7). The sequencing was performed using the IonGeneStudio S5 instrument, and the analysis was performed using the Ion Reporter and the Oncomine Knowledgebase Reporter software. Only genetic alterations with strong or potential clinical significance are reported. Patients with BRAF V600E mutations were started on dabrafenib combined with trametinib. Patients without targetable mutations received lenvatinib. For patients who were presented with rapidly progressing disease, lenvatinib was started empirically prior to the availability of NGS results. Treatment dosing was individualized according to the patient’s tolerance, co-morbidities, and clinical response. The starting dose of lenvatinib was 14–20 mg once daily, dabrafenib 150 mg twice daily, and trametinib 2 mg once daily, with dose adjustments according to patient tolerance.

Excluded from the analysis were patients who received TKIs with palliative intent and those with medullary thyroid cancer or undifferentiated thyroid cancer. Medical records were reviewed for demographic and clinical characteristics, molecular and genetic testing results, radiographic findings at diagnosis and following neoadjuvant therapy (to quantify tumor response), treatment details, and surgical outcomes. Radiologic response was evaluated by measuring the tumor size according to the RECIST 1.1 criteria (8) (complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD), and progressive disease (PD)).

Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) slides of pre-treatment samples and postoperative specimens were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for routine morphological evaluation. Immunohistochemistry staining was performed for CD31, ERG, and CD3. The slides were scanned using the Philips UFS scanner (Koninklijke Philips, The Netherlands). The pathologists, blinded to patient identifiers and their clinical outcomes, assessed the scanned slides and classified the following three parameters:
Pathologic response – given the absence of a thyroid-specific, standardized grading system for pathologic response to neoadjuvant therapy, response was assessed using a semi-quantitative residual viable tumor-based approach commonly applied across solid tumors (9). The entire tumor bed was extensively sampled and submitted for histopathologic evaluation. Pathologic response was determined by integrated assessment of treatment-related changes within the tumor bed, including fibrosis, necrosis, regression patterns, and the proportion of residual viable tumor cells (9). Pathologically complete response (pCR) was defined as no residual viable tumor cells. Patients with ≤10% residual viable tumor cells in the resected tumor bed were considered to have a major pathological response (mPR). A partial pathological response (pPR) was considered when ≤50% and >10% residual viable tumor cells were detected in the resected tumor bed. No pathological response (NPR) was defined as >50% residual viable tumor cells. Percent residual viable tumors were estimated across all submitted sections to provide a comprehensive assessment of response.
Lymphocytic infiltration, assessed by H&E-stained slides and by staining CD3.
Density of micro-vessels, assessed by staining the endothelial marker CD31.

sec.title: Study population and clinical outcomes
sec.p: Nine patients with advanced DTC who had received neoadjuvant therapy were included in the analysis. Their clinical characteristics and disease stage are shown in Table 1. Two of the patients had cT4b disease, and the others had lesions classified as cT4a. Six patients had regional lymph node metastases, and three patients had distal metastases involving the calvaria, clavicle, sternum, and lungs at presentation. Initial fine-needle aspiration confirmed that they all had DTC. The histologic type was papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in six patients, follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) in two patients, and oncocytic cell carcinoma (OCC) in one patient. The indications for neoadjuvant therapy are detailed in Table 1.

sec.p: Genetic sequencing revealed BRAF V600E mutations in two patients, who were treated accordingly with a combination of dabrafenib and trametinib. The other seven patients were treated with lenvatinib. Three of these seven patients presented with widespread tumor extent and severe symptoms (dyspnea or uncontrolled pain), necessitating treatment initiation prior to molecular characterization. Another four patients had no targetable mutation, with one case of TERT mutation and none with TP53. These results did not change treatment regimen. All study patients were assessed every 2–4 weeks for clinical response, and imaging was performed 3 months after treatment initiation to assess radiologic response and tumor resectability. The median duration of treatment was 5 months (range: 1–11).

The main adverse effects reported were fatigue (n = 3) and gastrointestinal disturbances (n = 3). There were no major adverse effects that required treatment cessation, but lenvatinib was temporarily stopped in two patients (one case due to bleeding into a calvarial metastasis, which was irradiated, and another case due to pancreatitis, which was treated). Lenvatinib treatment was cautiously re-initiated in lower doses in these two cases.

Imaging studies confirmed treatment response in eight cases (Fig. 1). One patient was treated with lenvatinib for only 1 month before tumor resection and did not have any imaging study to assess radiologic response preceding his surgery. None of these patients had progressed during the therapy: specifically, three patients had SD according to the RECIST 1.1 criteria and five patients had PR.

caption.p: Radiologic response according to the RECIST 1.1 criteria in eight patients who underwent imaging studies.

sec.p: All nine patients underwent curative intent surgical resection. Systemic therapy was stopped 7–10 days before surgery, as planned. Eight patients underwent total thyroidectomy, while the right lobe resection of the remaining patient was halted due to intraoperative loss of signal from the ipsilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lateral neck dissection was performed in cases in which metastatic lymph nodes were cytologically confirmed. No surgical adverse events could be attributed to the neoadjuvant regimen. One patient was tracheostomy-dependent postoperatively.

sec.title: Histologic changes
sec.p: Tumor necrosis and fibrosis comprised the major histologic patterns observed in the resected specimens after neoadjuvant therapy. These microscopic findings were mirrored by the macroscopic appearance of the thyroidectomy specimens, which frequently demonstrated replacement of normal thyroid parenchyma by firm white-tan tissue on gross examination. Areas of dense fibrosis and necrosis identified histologically corresponded to these firm, pale regions noted at the macroscopic level. Two patients had a major pathological response, and both were treated with lenvatinib. Figure 2 demonstrates the pathologic responses in all nine cases. Six of the nine tumors displayed necrosis and low proportion of residual viable tumor cells (10–25% of the tumor bed), including two cases classified as major pathological response. All six were treated with lenvatinib for at least 4 months. Fibrosis was evident in all nine tumors. The pathologic response did not correlate with either the histologic type of the cancer or the treatment duration. Figure 3 demonstrates representative images of H&E-stained sections of two patients before and after the treatment, as well as radiographic images that represent the radiologic response.

One patient was treated for 1 month with lenvatinib before surgical resection, and no imaging study was performed before surgery in that patient. mPR, major pathological response; pPR, partial pathological response; NA, not available.

sec.p: Lymphocytic infiltration varied considerably between specimens and was assessed descriptively due to marked heterogeneity. Abundant lymphocytic infiltration, occasionally with formation of lymphoid follicles, was observed in several tumors from patients treated with lenvatinib. Patients treated with dabrafenib and trametinib did not demonstrate similar lymphocytic infiltration (Fig. 4). Within the limitations of this small cohort, the extent of lymphocyte infiltration did not correlate with either dose or duration of neoadjuvant therapy or with the extent of the pathologic response.

caption.p: Lymphocytic infiltration following neoadjuvant therapy. Representative histologic and immunohistochemical images demonstrating differences in T-lymphocyte infiltration between tumors treated with lenvatinib and dabrafenib plus trametinib. Tumor specimen from a patient treated with lenvatinib showing stromal fibrosis and inflammatory cells infiltration on hematoxylin and eosin staining (A and B), and CD3 immunohistochemistry demonstrating prominent T-lymphocyte infiltration, predominantly within the tumor stroma with scattered intratumoral lymphocytes (C and D). Tumor specimen from a patient treated with dabrafenib plus trametinib showing tumor fibrosis on hematoxylin and eosin staining (E and F), with sparse CD3-positive T-lymphocytes on immunohistochemistry (G and H). Scale bars: 100 μm (A, C, E, G) and 200 μm (B, D, F, H).

sec.p: Decreased vessel density was observed in thyroid specimens following lenvatinib treatment. However, this was not noted in the two patients treated with dabrafenib and trametinib. Figure 5 demonstrates CD-31-stained sections before and after neoadjuvant therapy.

caption.p: Microvascular density following neoadjuvant therapy. Representative CD31 immunohistochemical staining highlighting tumor-associated microvasculature after neoadjuvant therapy. Tumor specimens from patients treated with lenvatinib (top panels) demonstrate reduced CD31-positive endothelial staining and decreased microvascular density. In contrast, specimens from patients treated with dabrafenib plus trametinib (bottom panels) show relatively preserved CD31-positive microvessels. CD31-positive endothelial cells are visualized as brown membranous staining outlining vascular structures. Scale bars as indicated.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Neoadjuvant therapy in advanced DTC is emerging as a beneficial strategy for unresectable disease or in cases at high risk of significant surgical morbidity. Recent studies have described the promising role of neoadjuvant therapy in enhancing resectability. One multicenter retrospective case series demonstrated that neoadjuvant treatment led to a significant reduction in surgical complexity scores, with 64.7% of patients proceeding to surgery and 58.8% achieving R0/R1 resections (10). Similarly, a single-institution study of nine patients demonstrated that neoadjuvant TKI therapy effectively downstaged their unresectable DTC or resectable DTC with unacceptable morbidities, enabling R0 resections without major surgical complications (11). Consistent with these observations, a recent multinational real-world study evaluated neoadjuvant multikinase and genotype-directed therapies across multiple thyroid cancer subtypes and demonstrated that surgical intervention became feasible in a substantial proportion of patients with DTC, with complete or near-complete resections achieved in the majority of operated cases (5).

The selection of systemic therapy remains subject to physician’s discretion in the neoadjuvant setting. While BRAF-targeted therapies, such as combined dabrafenib and trametinib, are clearly indicated for BRAF V600E-mutant tumors, patients without targetable mutations typically receive multitarget TKIs. Among the latter, lenvatinib is often the preferred first-line agent due to its high response rate and rapid tumor regression capacity, as previously demonstrated in radioiodine-refractory DTC (3). Lenvatinib acts by inhibiting vascular endothelial cell growth factor receptors (VEGFRs) and multiple vascular endothelial cell growth factor derivatives, thereby inhibiting angiogenesis. Dabrafenib specifically targets BRAF V600E and inhibits cell growth, while trametinib inhibits MEK1 and MEK2 in the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway to suppress downstream signaling (12).

In our series, lenvatinib was well tolerated and associated with tumor volume regression as seen on radiologic evaluation. It also induced major pathological response in two cases. These findings suggest that lenvatinib may be particularly advantageous for advanced, non-BRAF-mutated DTC in the neoadjuvant setting.

This study revealed several histopathologic changes that illustrated the effect of the administered drug regimen. While lenvatinib showed antitumor effects, such as decreased vascularization and increased inflammatory cell infiltration, dabrafenib and trametinib resulted predominantly in fibrosis and necrosis of the tumor. Okubo et al. (13) reported lenvatinib-associated microvascular damage that was demarcated by decreased microvascular density. A similar therapeutic effect was observed in our cohort, characterized by a decrease in microvessel density in the thyroid specimens following neoadjuvant lenvatinib treatment (Fig. 5). Notably, these specific histopathologic changes were not observed in the two patients treated with dabrafenib and trametinib. Our results, in conjunction with previous studies, highlight the distinct histopathologic changes induced by lenvatinib; however, the small sample size limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions and underscores the necessity for more comprehensive, larger-scale studies.

One of the more intriguing findings that emerged from our study is the histologic evidence of greater immune infiltration following lenvatinib therapy. Although lenvatinib is primarily known for its antiangiogenic effects, recent studies have shown that it also modulates the tumor immune microenvironment, potentially enhancing antitumor immunity (14). The increased lymphoid infiltration and formation of lymphoid follicles observed in our lenvatinib-treated patients suggest a role for immune activation as part of its therapeutic effect, even in the absence of concurrent immunotherapy. In a study by Yamauchi et al. (15), lenvatinib was shown to induce immuno-activation that resulted from VEGFR and fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) blockade. Those authors suggest that FGF–FGFR signaling plays an important role in both tumor angiogenesis and antitumor immunity and that it may also be involved in resistance to VEGF inhibition. Dual blockade of VEGF and FGF signaling by lenvatinib might, therefore, be advantageous as a potentiator of immunotherapy. In contrast, BRAF-targeted therapies did not demonstrate similar immune changes in our cohort, aligning with preclinical data indicating differing mechanisms of action. These findings raise the possibility of future combination strategies involving lenvatinib and immune checkpoint inhibitors, even in the neoadjuvant setting. While these findings align with emerging evidence regarding the pro-immunogenic properties of multitarget TKIs, such as lenvatinib, their direct impact on clinical outcomes in the neoadjuvant setting remains to be further elucidated in a larger prospective cohort.

A key clinical challenge is determining the optimal duration of neoadjuvant therapy. In our cohort, treatment lasted a median of 5 months, with some variability based upon tolerability and clinical response. While longer durations may potentially promote better pathologic responses, prolonged TKI exposure can increase toxicity and may complicate surgery by therapy-induced fibrosis and adhesions. We observed that lenvatinib had induced meaningful tumor regression within a limited timeframe. Nevertheless, there is no standardized timeline for proceeding to surgery. Ultimately, our findings underscore the need for larger, well-established prospective studies to determine the exact optimal timing for neoadjuvant intervention in advanced DTC. Imaging, including metabolic imaging, can assess tumor size, intertumoral changes related to systemic therapy, and resectability; however, certain studies, such as restricted diffusion in magnetic resonance sequences, can possibly lead to misunderstanding of the tumor viability.

A critical observation in our study is the imperfect correlation between radiologic and histopathologic responses. While eight of our study patients showed radiologic PR or SD, only two demonstrated major pathological response. One patient did not undergo post-treatment imaging prior to surgery due to clinical intolerance that necessitated surgical intervention; consequently, this patient was excluded from the radiologic response assessment while remaining valuable for pathologic response. This discordance between radiologic and pathologic responses is well documented in other tumor types and may reflect the inability of RECIST criteria to capture non-size-based indicators of treatment efficacy, such as necrosis or fibrosis (16). Therefore, reliance upon imaging alone may underestimate the therapeutic impact and its utility for determining the duration of neoadjuvant therapy and timing of surgery remains limited.

This study is limited by its small sample size and retrospective nature. The small sample size (9 patients) and heterogeneity of tumor characteristics and neoadjuvant treatments limit the generalizability of our findings and the ability to draw definitive conclusions or derive broadly applicable clinical recommendations. Accordingly, our findings should be interpreted cautiously and viewed as hypothesis-generating within the context of an exploratory analysis. Nonetheless, this study provides interesting evidence on the pathologic response to neoadjuvant systemic therapy in advanced DTC. As the neoadjuvant treatment becomes more widely adopted for thyroid cancer, treatment protocols are likely to become standardized, warranting exploration of combination therapies that exploit both targeted and immunomodulatory mechanisms.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Pathologic evaluation of neoadjuvant therapy in advanced DTC provides mechanistic insights and underscores its benefits beyond tumor volume reduction, simply measurable by radiologic studies. Notably, our preliminary observations suggest distinct therapy-specific responses, such as vascular remodeling and immune infiltration following lenvatinib treatment, compared to a predominance of fibrosis in patients treated with dabrafenib/trametinib. While these findings suggest potential mechanistic differences, further studies with larger cohorts are required to confirm these patterns. These findings support the potential of lenvatinib as a neoadjuvant agent with immunomodulatory effects and point to opportunities for future combination strategies with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Standardization of treatment duration and integration of histopathologic assessment may optimize surgical timing and enhance patient outcomes.
